1F (Linear Algebra)

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 165
1F OurBigBook.com
Put q=(1,1,1,1)T and arrange the four vectors as the columns of A=(x−1)I+qqT. On the one-dimensional vector subspace spanned by q, the eigenvalue is x+3. On the three-dimensional orthogonal complement q⊥={v:∑i​vi​=0}, the eigenvalue is x−1. Thus
detA=(x+3)(x−1)3,
(1)
and the vectors fail to be a basis exactly when x=1 or x=−3.
For x=1, all four columns equal q. The matrix rank is 1, a basis of their span is {q}, and an extension to a basis of R4 is
{q,e1​,e2​,e3​}.​
(2)
The last coordinate first forces the coefficient of q to vanish in any linear dependence, after which the other coefficients vanish.
For x=−3, the matrix rank is 3 and the span is exactly q⊥. A basis consists of the first three original columns,
{(−3,1,1,1),(1,−3,1,1),(1,1,−3,1)}.​
(3)
Indeed, writing them as q−4ei​, a vanishing linear combination has coefficient sum zero by its fourth coordinate, and then each coefficient is zero by the first three coordinates. Adjoin q to extend this basis to R4, since q∈/q⊥.

2E (Groups, Rings and Modules)

Words: 201 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 201
2E OurBigBook.com
Eisenstein's criterion. Let f(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[X] be a nonconstant primitive polynomial. If a prime number p satisfies p∤an​, p∣aj​ for 0≤j<n, and p2∤a0​, then f is an irreducible polynomial over Q.
To prove the Eisenstein criterion, suppose a nontrivial factorization exists over Q. Gauss lemma for polynomials gives f=gh with g,h∈Z[X] of positive degree. Their leading coefficients are not divisible by p, because their product is an​. Reduction modulo p therefore preserves both degrees, and
g​h=an​​Xnin Fp​[X].
(4)
Since the only irreducible factor of the right side is X, both reduced factors are nonzero monomials of positive degree. Their constant coefficients are consequently divisible by p. This would make p2∣g(0)h(0)=a0​, a contradiction.
For the requested polynomial, shift the variable by one. The binomial theorem gives
Φp​(X+1)=X(X+1)p−1​=∑j=1p​(jp​)Xj−1.
(5)
It is monic, all coefficients below the leading one are divisible by p, and the constant coefficient is p, not divisible by p2. The Eisenstein criterion proves irreducibility of this shifted polynomial. The substitution X↦X+1 is an automorphism of Q[X], with inverse X↦X−1, so it preserves nontrivial factorizations. Hence
Xp−1+Xp−2+⋯+1 is irreducible over Q.​
(6)
This is the cyclotomic polynomial for a prime index.

A contraction mapping on a metric space (X,d) is a map f:X→X for which there is a single constant q with 0≤q<1 such that
d(f(x),f(y))≤qd(x,y)for every x,y∈X.​
(7)
The same q must work for every pair. Merely decreasing each nonzero distance strictly does not suffice for this definition.

b

Words: 83 Articles: 1
3G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
b OurBigBook.com
The contraction mapping theorem states that a contraction mapping of a nonempty complete metric space into itself has a unique fixed point x∗​. For any starting point x0​, the iterates xn+1​=f(xn​) converge to x∗​, with the quantitative estimate
d(xn​,x∗​)≤1−qqn​d(x1​,x0​).​
(8)
Completeness and the self-map condition are essential: the geometric estimate makes the iterates a Cauchy sequence, completeness supplies their limit in X, and continuity of the contraction mapping makes that limit a fixed point. If two fixed points existed, their distance would be at most q times itself, forcing equality of the points.

c OurBigBook.com
Define Fi​(x)=ai​+61​∑j=i​sinxj​. Solving the system is equivalent to finding a fixed point of F:R3→R3. The mean value theorem implies ∣sinu−sinv∣≤∣u−v∣. In the specified metric,
d(F(x),F(y))​≤61​i=1∑3​j=i∑​∣xj​−yj​∣=31​j=1∑3​∣xj​−yj​∣=31​d(x,y).​
(9)
Each coordinate difference occurs exactly twice. This metric makes R3 a nonempty complete metric space, because a Cauchy sequence in it is Cauchy in each real coordinate, and coordinate convergence implies convergence in the sum metric. Thus F is a contraction mapping with constant 1/3.
There is exactly one solution for every choice of (a1​,a2​,a3​), by the contraction mapping theorem. Iteration of F from any starting vector also constructs it.

Words: 172 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 172
4G OurBigBook.com
Rouché's theorem. Suppose f,g are holomorphic functions on a neighbourhood of the closure of a bounded domain enclosed by a simple, positively oriented, piecewise smooth curve. If ∣g(z)∣<∣f(z)∣ on the boundary, then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside, counted with multiplicity.
Apply Rouche theorem with f(z)=z4+3 and g(z)=eiz on the first-quadrant quarter-disc of radius R=2​. On the two radial segments, z4 is nonnegative real, so ∣f∣≥3, whereas ∣g∣=e−Imz≤1. On the circular arc,
∣f(z)∣≥∣z∣4−3=1.
(10)
At every arc point with positive imaginary part, ∣g∣<1, giving the strict inequality; at the remaining endpoint z=R, ∣f∣=7>1=∣g∣. Thus the strict boundary inequality holds everywhere, including the origin.
The four zeros of f have modulus 31/4 and arguments π/4,3π/4,5π/4,7π/4. Exactly one lies inside the chosen domain. Rouche theorem gives exactly one zero of f+g there, counted with multiplicity, so that zero is simple. Finally any zero in the open first quadrant satisfies
∣z∣4=∣3+eiz∣≤3+e−Imz<4.
(11)
There can be no additional zero outside the quarter-disc. Hence
Exactly one zero lies in the first quadrant, and ∣z0​∣<2​.​
(12)

a0​=π2​∫0π​x2dx=32π2​.

Twice applying integration by parts gives, for n≥1,
∫0π​x2cos(nx)dx​=−n2​∫0π​xsin(nx)dx=n22π(−1)n​,an​=n24(−1)n​.​

Therefore the periodic Fourier representation is
x2=3π2​+4n=1∑∞​n2(−1)ncos(nx)​,−π≤x≤π,​

with periodic continuation. The periodic extension is continuous, including the identified endpoints, and piecewise smooth, so the Fourier series converges to it. The coefficients also give absolute convergence and uniform convergence by comparison with ∑n−2.
At x=π, the cosine cancels the alternating coefficient sign; at x=0, it is identically one. These evaluations yield
n=1∑∞​n21​=6π2​,n=1∑∞​n2(−1)n+1​=12π2​.​

The orbital angular momentum linear operator is the cross product of the position operator and the momentum operator:
L=r×p​,Li​=j,k∑​εijk​xj​p​k​.​
(17)
In position space, p​=−iℏ∇, so L=−iℏr×∇. The Levi-Civita symbol gives L1​=x2​p​3​−x3​p​2​ and its cyclic analogues.

Use the canonical commutation relations [xi​,xj​]=[p​i​,p​j​]=0 and [xi​,p​j​]=iℏδij​I. For compactness write products without hats in the calculation, on a common domain such as smooth compactly supported wavefunctions. Expanding the commutator gives
[L1​,L2​]=[x2​p3​,x3​p1​]−[x2​p3​,x1​p3​]−[x3​p2​,x3​p1​]+[x3​p2​,x1​p3​].
(18)
The middle two commutators vanish because all the relevant indices differ. The first is −iℏx2​p1​, since [p3​,x3​]=−iℏI; the last is iℏx1​p2​, since [x3​,p3​]=iℏI. Thus
[L1​,L2​]=iℏ(x1​p​2​−x2​p​1​)=iℏL3​.​
(19)
This is one of the orbital angular momentum commutation relations.

[L1​,L22​][L1​,L32​][L1​,L12​]​=iℏ(L3​L2​+L2​L3​),=−iℏ(L2​L3​+L3​L2​),=0.​

⟨L1​⟩ψ​=⟨ψ,ψ⟩⟨ψ,L1​ψ⟩​=ℏcos2ωt+3sin2ωtcos2ωt−3sin2ωt​.

∇⋅E=0,∇⋅B=0,∇×E=−∂t​B,∇×B=μ0​ϵ0​∂t​E.
(24)
Take the curl of Faraday's law and use the curl of the curl identity ∇×(∇×E)=∇(∇⋅E)−∇2E. The divergence term vanishes by Gauss's law, while the time derivative of the magnetic curl supplies −μ0​ϵ0​∂t2​E. Thus
c21​∂t2​E−∇2E=0,∇⋅E=0,c=(ϵ0​μ0​)−1/2.​
(25)
This is the transverse electromagnetic wave equation.

ω2=c2k2.​

B(z,t)=2​ωkE0​​(−1,1,0)cos(kz−ωt).​
(27)
For ω=ck, its amplitude is E0​/c. The magnetic field, electric field and direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular. A constant background magnetic field could be added; the expression above is the wave-associated field.

a OurBigBook.com
Apply the numerical method to the scalar test equation y′=λy, with z=hλ. Its linear stability domain consists of those z∈C for which the discrete solution stays bounded as the step count tends to infinity. For a one-step method with stability function R, this is
S={z:∣R(z)∣≤1}.​
(30)
If asymptotic decay is required, use ∣R(z)∣<1 instead; this only changes the boundary conventions in part (b). A method is A-stable if its stability domain contains the left half-plane, so every decaying linear test equation is stable for every positive step size. For a multistep method, the corresponding definition uses the root condition for a multistep method for every characteristic root, including simplicity of unit-modulus roots.

Expand the second stage by the Taylor theorem, writing f=f(tn​,yn​) and Dy​f for the derivative in the state variable:
k2​=f+2h​(ft​+(Dy​f)f)+O(h2).
(31)
The update therefore agrees with the exact solution's Taylor series:
yn+1​=yn​+hf+2h2​(ft​+(Dy​f)f)+O(h3).
(32)
Thus the one-step local truncation error is O(h3), and the method has order at least two under the usual smoothness and Lipschitz continuity assumptions.
For f=λy, the two-stage Runge-Kutta method gives
R(z)=1+z+2z2​.​
(33)
On the real axis, R(z)=21​(z+1)2+21​≥21​, so ∣R(z)∣≤1 is equivalent to (z+1)2≤1. Hence
S∩R=[−2,0].​
(34)
The decay convention gives (−2,0). Since negative real values such as z=−3 lie outside the linear stability domain, the method is not A-stable. Its order is exactly two, since R(z) lacks the cubic term of ez.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
If there are i balls in box A, a ball currently in B is selected with probability (k−i)/k, increasing the count, and a ball in A is selected with probability i/k, decreasing it. For k≥1,
Pi,i+1​=kk−i​ (0≤i<k),Pi,i−1​=ki​ (0<i≤k),​
(35)
with every other transition zero. This is the Ehrenfest urn model.
The stationary distribution is
πi​=2−k(ik​),0≤i≤k.​
(36)
It is normalized by the binomial theorem, and it obeys the detailed balance:
πi​Pi,i+1​=2−k(ik​)kk−i​=2−k(i+1k​)ki+1​=πi+1​Pi+1,i​.
(37)
All other pairs have zero flux in both directions. These identities prove stationarity and show that this is a reversible Markov chain in equilibrium. The finite chain is irreducible and has period two; reversibility does not require aperiodicity.

b

Words: 83 Articles: 1
9H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
b OurBigBook.com
A finite irreducible Markov chain is positive recurrent. Its mean recurrence time to state i, starting at i and counting the first positive return, is 1/πi​. This identity comes from the long-run fraction of time spent at that state: successive return cycles each contain one visit at their start, so the fraction is the reciprocal of the mean cycle length. It remains valid for a periodic chain.
Here π0​=2−k, hence
E0​[T]=2k minutes.​
(38)
For k=1 the return is deterministically after two minutes, which checks the formula.

The algebraic dual map is δ=α∨:W∗→V∗, defined by δ(φ)=φ∘α. The annihilator of a vector subspace U⊆V is
U∘={λ∈V∗:λ(u)=0 for all u∈U}.
(39)
Every functional φ∘α vanishes on kerα, so imδ⊆(kerα)∘. Conversely, let λ∈(kerα)∘. Define a functional on imα by λ(αv)=λ(v). It is well defined because two preimages differ by an element of kerα. Extend a basis of imα to one of W and extend the functional arbitrarily, for instance by zero on the extra basis vectors. The resulting φ∈W∗ satisfies δφ=λ.
This is the dual image and kernel annihilator identity. Therefore
imδ=(kerα)∘.​
(40)
The basis extension theorem also gives dimU∘=dimV−dimU. By the rank-nullity theorem,
dimimδ=dimV−dimkerα=dimimα.​
(41)
Apply rank-nullity theorem to both maps, using dimW∗=dimW, to obtain
dimkerα−dimkerδ=dimV−dimW.​
(42)
Over C, this is the algebraic dual, without complex conjugation; the adjoint operator in part (b) uses the inner products instead.

The adjoint operator α∗:W→V is uniquely characterized by
⟨αv,w⟩W​=⟨v,α∗w⟩V​for all v,w.
(43)
Let A=ββ∗+γ∗γ:V→V. Its quadratic form is nonnegative:
⟨Av,v⟩=∥β∗v∥2+∥γv∥2.
(44)
If Av=0, both norms vanish. In particular v∈kerγ=imβ, while β∗v=0 means v is orthogonal to imβ, by the defining adjoint operator identity. A vector belonging to a vector subspace and its orthogonal complement must be zero. Hence A is injective, and finite dimensionality makes it surjective.
Thus
ββ∗+γ∗γ is an isomorphism of V.​
(45)
The same calculation shows it is a positive-definite operator when V={0}.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Work with the usual commutative unital Noetherian ring convention. First prove that every submodule of Rd is a finitely generated module. For d=1, a submodule is an ideal, hence finitely generated by Noetherianity. For the induction step, project a submodule N⊆Rd onto its last coordinate. Its image is a finitely generated ideal; choose lifts in N of its generators. The projection kernel lies in Rd−1 and is finitely generated by induction. The kernel generators together with the chosen lifts generate N, since subtracting a combination of the lifts leaves an element of the kernel.
Now choose a surjection Rd→M from a finite generating set of the module M. For any submodule U⊆M, its inverse image in Rd is finitely generated by the result just proved. The images of those generators generate U.
Every submodule of M is finitely generated. In particular M is a Noetherian module: the union of an ascending chain is a submodule, and its finite generators all belong to a single member of the chain, forcing eventual stabilization.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Let P=Ann(m) be maximal among annihilators of nonzero elements of M. It is a proper ideal, since 1m=m=0. Suppose ab∈P and b∈/P. Then bm=0 and
P⊆Ann(bm),a∈Ann(bm).
(46)
The inclusion holds because every r∈P satisfies r(bm)=b(rm)=0. Maximality in the stated set forces Ann(bm)=P, so a∈P. This proves the defining implication for a prime ideal:
ab∈P ⟹ a∈P or b∈P.​
(47)
This is a maximal annihilator of a module element is prime argument. Maximality among element annihilators is sufficient; P need not be a maximal ideal of R.

Solution

Words: 137
c OurBigBook.com
If M=0, take the empty filtration. Otherwise a nonzero quotient Q=M/Mi​ is a finitely generated module. Because R has the ascending chain condition on ideals, the nonempty collection of annihilators of nonzero elements of Q has a maximal element. Part (b), applied to Q, supplies q=0 with a prime ideal P=Ann(q).
The map R→Rq, r↦rq, is surjective with kernel P. The first isomorphism theorem gives Rq≅R/P. Let Mi+1​ be the inverse image of Rq under M→Q. Then
Mi​⊊Mi+1​,Mi+1​/Mi​≅R/P.​
(48)
Repeat whenever the quotient remains nonzero. An infinite repetition would give a strictly ascending chain of submodules of the Noetherian module M, contradicting part (a). Thus the process stops after finitely many steps, necessarily at M.
This constructs the required prime filtration 0=M0​⊊⋯⊊Ml​=M, with each successive quotient R/Pi​ for a prime Pi​.

Two norms N1​,N2​ on the same vector space are equivalent norms, or Lipschitz equivalent, if there are constants 0<c≤C<∞ such that cN1​(v)≤N2​(v)≤CN1​(v) for every v. The constants are uniform over the whole space.
Let N be any norm on Rn. The triangle inequality and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality give
N(x)≤∑i​∣xi​∣N(ei​)≤(∑i​N(ei​)2)1/2∥x∥2​=C∥x∥2​.
(49)
The reverse triangle inequality then gives ∣N(x)−N(y)∣≤C∥x−y∥2​, so N is Euclidean-continuous; this continuity was derived, rather than assumed. On the compact Euclidean unit sphere, N attains a strictly positive minimum c, because it vanishes only at zero. Homogeneity yields
c∥x∥2​≤N(x)≤C∥x∥2​.​
(50)
Finally a linear map A:Rn→Rm satisfies ∥Ax∥2​≤(∑i,j​∣aij​∣2)1/2∥x∥2​, again by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The equivalence just proved transfers this bound to any norms on the source and target. Hence every such linear map is continuous.

A quotient topological space of a topological space X is obtained by an equivalence relation ∼: its points are the classes X/∼, and the canonical surjection is q(x)=[x]. The quotient topology declares a subset U of the quotient open exactly when q−1(U) is open in X. More generally a surjection onto a set specifies the same topology by this condition.
For a Hausdorff source with a non-Hausdorff quotient, use X=R and x∼y when x−y∈Q. Any nonempty open inverse image is a nonempty open subset of R invariant under rational translations. It contains an interval I, and for every real t there is a rational r with t−r∈I; hence it contains every t. Thus R/Q has the indiscrete topology.
It has distinct points, for instance the classes of 0 and 2​, but neither has a proper nonempty open neighbourhood. The quotient is not Hausdorff, even though R is a Hausdorff space.

This union is open in R2, so U is open by the quotient topology. Distinct integer lattice vectors are at least distance one apart, whereas 2r<1. Thus these open balls are disjoint, with a positive gap between any two.
Each ball is connected, since it is convex. It is both open and closed relative to the displayed union: its complement there is the union of all the other open balls. No connected component can meet two such relatively separated pieces. Consequently the components are exactly the infinitely many balls B(u+m,r). Translation by −m is a homeomorphism from each component onto B(u,r). The statement uses the intended positive radius 0<r<1/2.

Two lie within 1/N; taking their difference and, if needed, its negative yields an integer multiple of α with fractional part δ∈(0,1/N). The multiples 0,δ,…,⌊1/δ⌋δ form a 1/N-net of the circle and are themselves integer multiples of α modulo one. Taking N arbitrarily large proves density.

where g(d)=P(∣(Z+n​d)/W/(n−2)​∣>tn−2,0.975​). This is also the noncentral t-distribution description of the power. As explained in part (a), an exact residual-based test requires n>2.

Solution

Words: 290
a OurBigBook.com
A maximum flow problem specifies a finite directed flow network, a source s, a sink t, and nonnegative arc capacities. A feasible flow assigns 0≤fe​≤ce​ to each arc, with incoming flow equal to outgoing flow at each vertex other than s,t. The objective is to maximize the net flow leaving s, equivalently entering t.
The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm starts with zero flow. Its residual network has a forward arc of capacity ce​−fe​ and a reverse arc of capacity fe​ for each original arc. If an s–t path has positive residual capacities, augment by their minimum: increase flow along forward arcs and decrease it along reverse arcs. This preserves capacity bounds and conservation, and increases the flow value by that positive bottleneck. Repeat until there is no augmenting path.
For rational capacities, choose a positive integer D clearing every denominator. Initially all flows and residual capacities are integer multiples of 1/D, and augmentation preserves that property. Every augmentation therefore increases the flow value by at least 1/D. The flow value is bounded above by the sum of capacities of arcs leaving s. Thus only finitely many augmentations can occur, independently of how the augmenting paths are chosen.
To see why termination supplies a maximum, let S consist of vertices reachable from s in the final residual network. The sink is not in S. Each original arc from S to its complement is saturated; each original arc entering S has zero flow, since otherwise its reverse residual arc would leave S. The resulting flow value equals the capacity of this cut. No feasible flow exceeds a cut capacity. Hence the algorithm terminates at a maximum flow for rational capacities, proving the relevant max-flow min-cut theorem conclusion as well.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
An extreme point of a convex set cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct members. If a permutation matrix P=θB+(1−θ)C with 0<θ<1 and B,C doubly stochastic, each zero entry of P forces the corresponding entries of B,C to be zero by nonnegativity. The unique possible nonzero entry in each row must then be one by the row sum. Thus B=C=P, proving that every permutation matrix is extreme.
Conversely, let A be a doubly stochastic matrix that is not a permutation matrix. At least one entry lies strictly between zero and one. Form a bipartite graph whose two vertex classes are rows and columns, with edges precisely at these fractional entries. Every incident row has at least two fractional entries: a single fractional entry, with all other entries zero or one, could not give row sum one. The same holds for columns.
A finite nonempty graph whose incident vertices all have degree at least two contains a cycle. In a bipartite graph that cycle has even length. Assign alternating signs +1,−1 to its entries, giving a nonzero matrix D with every row and column sum zero. Choose ε>0 smaller than the distance of each cycle entry from both zero and one. Then A+εD and A−εD remain doubly stochastic matrices, are distinct, and satisfy
A=21​(A+εD)+21​(A−εD).
(107)
So A is not extreme. Therefore
Ext(C)={permutation matrices}.​
(108)
This alternating-cycle perturbation of a doubly stochastic matrix proves the extreme-point part of the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem directly.
